direction: Narrow the contribution to what survives the overlap: (a) a retrieval-agnostic temporal relevance layer whose temporal signal is valid-time (as-of) membership rather than elapsed-time decay, (b) evaluated as a base-retriever x signal-form factorial (BM25, dense, hybrid) with a version-level contamination metric as a primary outcome and queries deliberately decoupled from recency, and (c) a version-level benchmark of amended statutes/regulations with near-duplicate successive versions and ground-truth in-force clauses. Drop the claims that temporal decay, temporal validity, or architecture-agnostic treatment are themselves novel, and drop answer accuracy as the sole success criterion.
hypothesis: For time-specific queries over continuously amended regulatory text, an explicitly valid-time-aware, retrieval-agnostic re-ranking layer reduces retrieval of superseded or not-yet-in-force near-duplicate clauses and improves answer accuracy relative to the same base retriever with semantic similarity alone, and outperforms elapsed-time decay; the size of the gain depends on the base retriever and on how often the authoritative version is not the most recent.
rationale: The evidence shows the original framing is largely pre-empted: semantic-plus-exponential-decay hybrid retrieval with a temporal benchmark is published, learnable decay in retrieval is published, the valid-time/bitemporal requirement is already articulated in legal-retrieval theory, a legal benchmark encoding temporal validity exists, and a legal RAG system already filters sources by temporal validity. What is not covered anywhere found is (1) an empirical cross-retriever transfer study of a temporal layer, (2) version-level contamination measurement on near-duplicate amended legal clauses, and (3) a measured comparison of recency decay against valid-time membership on such a corpus, with queries decoupled from recency. The original mechanism (elapsed-time decay) is also the weakest part on independent grounds, since a superseded clause can be the temporally nearest one. Narrowing scope this way keeps a testable, non-pre-empted contribution while fixing the mechanism; it deserves investigation next because it can be falsified cheaply and would still produce a useful negative result about when temporal re-ranking helps.
research_question: Does an explicit valid-time (as-of) temporal relevance layer, applied post hoc to standard sparse, dense and hybrid retrievers, reduce retrieval of superseded or not-yet-in-force near-duplicate legal clauses and improve answer accuracy for time-specific queries over continuously amended regulatory text, compared with semantic-only retrieval, elapsed-time decay, and a hard as-of filter?
